Mr. Speaker, my intervention concerns homeless people. Unlike Britain and Australia, Canada has no legislation to define government responsibility with respect to the obligation to shelter the homeless. The United States are now considering the possibility of passing such legislation, despite the pronouncements of the Reagan administration. In Canada this obligation does not exist at either government level, federal or provincial. In the meantime the federal and provincial administrations are throwing the ball back and forth in their respective courts.
What matters is to secure a commitment to settle the problem of homeless people in the next few years, particularly before winter sets in. If nobody is held responsible the problem will not be solved and the solutions advocated will not be co-ordinated, very likely leading to yet another waste of public funds.
I therefore urge the Canadian Government to define government responsibility. Homeless people are already on the fringe of society. Does the Government want to integrate them? Where is the political will?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, perhaps the most famous Canadian in history died last Friday. I am sure all Members of this House would want to join me in paying tribute to Lome Greene. A generation of Americans and Canadians, indeed millions of people around the world, grew up believing that Lome Greene was Ben Cartwright, that somewhat stern but altogether wholesome father figure in the Bonanza series on American television.
That was undoubtedly his most famous role in which he was reputedly seen by 400 million people a week.
Lome Greene was more than that, however. He was the son of Russian immigrant parents and grew up here in Ottawa where his father was a shoemaker. He began his interest in theatre in the early 1930s when he attended Queen's University. After graduation and further study in New York he joined the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation as an actor but within three months was hired as the announcer on the national news.
During the war years I remember, as countless other millions of Canadians will, hearing Lome Greene tell us of the latest troop movements, the latest catastrophe, and the latest triumph, in that deep sombre voice which was his trademark. He was called "The Voice of Doom", and an entire country listened.
He was also devoted to talent. He started his own school for announcers in Toronto and was a respected classical actor both on Broadway and at Stratford. He starred in many television series and plays.
Although he lived in Hollywood he never forgot his Canadian roots. He was constantly seeking opportunities for young Canadian artists and actors. I personally know that during the 1984 Olympics Lome extended his good wishes, help, and active participation in Los Angeles to aid our athletes there.
Having known Lome personally I know that he enjoyed the respect and affection of all his colleagues and the admiration of followers and fans everywhere. Just as he never forgot Canada in all his years in the United States, I am sure Canadians will never forget him. On behalf of myself personally and millions of Canadians, I extend to his family our heartfelt condolences. We assure them that we will never forget Ben Cartwright, or Lome Greene.
Hear, hear!

subtopic: OPENING OF GLENBURN CO-OPERATIVE HOME IN TORONTO
OPENING OF GLENBURN CO-OPERATIVE HOME IN TORONTO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, ironically, while hundreds of Metro Toronto residents were lining up for hours yesterday hoping for a chance to buy an expensive and yet-to-be-built house, I was attending the official opening of the Glenburn Co-operative Home in my riding which was established to provide affordable housing for low and moderate income families.
The six-storey 50-unit apartment building, long the subject of maintenance complaints from residents and neighbours alike, has now been completely renovated by the initiative of the former tenants who bought the building and turned it into a non-profit co-op with financial assistance from the federal Government through CMHC.


The Glenburn Co-op is an excellent example of how residents working together with government can provide desperately needed affordable housing. We need a lot more of the same.

Mr. Speaker, last night CBC provided a national broadcast forum for the Ambassador from South Africa. We heard the official voice of a land in which the voices of both the press and the oppressed are silenced. Thus we replay for this reincarnated Nazi regime the innocent collusion of the thirties that allowed the propagandists of Hitler to shield us from the Holocaust. What is happening here?
A people are oppressed and we raise the ogre of Marxism as if the political philosophy of the victims of any oppression is of relevance to the justice of their cause.
A people are jailed, tortured, mutilated and killed by a regime that denies them their very humanity, and we say that the use of violence by the oppressed should not be condoned while the West's inaction condones the violence of the oppressor.
A victimized people turns against collaborators and demonstrates that the denial of humanity will breed inhumanity, and again we condemn the victims, forgetting the fate of traitors at the hands of European mobs in 1945. What is happening here?
Are we being led to a lessening resolve in our support of democracy in southern Africa? Is our Government abandoning its promises? Is our Foreign Minister now, after returning from Africa, prepared to seek compromise with South Africa and those other Governments which profit from apartheid in order to preserve, in southern Africa and for the world, peace in our time"?

Mr. Speaker, like the Right Hon. Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Turner), I am sure that all Canadians and Members of the House will join me in extending our condolences to the family of Lome Greene, a great Canadian.
Mr. Greene was and will remain a superb role model for all Canadians who wish to achieve success on an international level. Mr. Greene became one of Hollywood's most prominent
Canadians, yet he was so proud of his Canadian roots that he retained his Canadian citizenship despite all the success the United States had brought him.
Last year Mr. Greene stated: "I feel close to Canada". He returned to Canada to film and produce a television series on CTV called Lome Greene's New Wilderness.
He has left us with a standard of love and loyalty for Canada of which we certainly can be proud. With his passing Canada has lost one of its greatest ambassadors-at-large.
Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Mr. Brian Tobin (Humber-Port au Port-St. Barbe):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last week the NDP endorsed the position that sometimes a resort to violence is absolutely essential in the struggle against apartheid. Over the weekend the NDP dumped the Member who put that position and at the same time restated this pro-violence position.
May I humbly suggest that they have it backwards. They ought to have dropped the pro-violence position and retained the critic, who at least raised this important question and brought the NDP out of the shadows.
Every Member of Parliament can empathize with the feelings of those who in frustration may be driven to consider the use of violence to obtain fundamental justice. However, as much as we may seek to understand the seeds of violence, we must never condone it.
All over the world there are those with causes who seek to legitimize the power of the gun, the use of violence in obtaining their ends.
Violence begets violence in South Africa, the Middle East, Central and South America, Asia, Europe, or indeed North America. We cannot pick and choose, whether it be the PLO, the IRA, the Contras, the ANC, the Basques separatists, or the FLQ. Our response in this Chamber must be a resounding no to violence.

Mr. Speaker, it is now three years since the Progressive Conservative Government was elected. In those three years, Canada has had the strongest economic growth record among all industrialized countries.


The results are now in for the period ending June 30. In the 12 months ending June 30, Canada had the strongest economic growth. In the 24 months ending June 30, Canada had the strongest economic growth. In the 36 months ending June 30, the entire period of the Government, Canada had the strongest economic growth among industrialized countries.
Not only did we have the strongest economic growth, we have had the largest proportionate increase in employment among all industrialized countries for the last 12 months, the last 24 months, and the last 36 months.
Indeed, when we formed the Government I recall the Leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broadbent) suggesting that the Government should take on an unemployment reduction target. The target he would be happy to set for himself would be a 1 per cent reduction in unemployment each year.
At the time we became the Government, the unemployment rate was 11.7 per cent. At the end of the first year, the average unemployment rate was 10.5 per cent. At the end of our third year, the average unemployment rate was 9.6 per cent. We have met that target set by the NDP Leader in terms of reduction of unemployment.

The Toronto Star today reported a very interesting poll. Canadians across the country were asked if they felt the country's economy was better off now than three years ago. In every region of the country except one; in Atlantic Canada, in Quebec, in the Prairies and British Columbia, an overwhelming number of Canadians recognized the job the Government was doing.
In Ontario the results indicated that only 44 per cent felt the Canadian economy was strong. I wonder whether the results do not indicate that the reporting of The Toronto Star itself is part of the reason Canadians do not understand the impressive growth we have had over this last three years.

subtopic: INDIA-INTERROGATION OF CANADIAN CHARGED WITH SMUGGLING WEAPONS
INDIA-INTERROGATION OF CANADIAN CHARGED WITH SMUGGLING WEAPONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a young Canadian of the Sikh faith has been charged with weapons smuggling in India. He is reported to have made a full confession after five days of rigorous interrogation by Indian anti-terrorist forces. This report appeared about the same time the Canadian Security Intelligence Service was admitting it had used false information to put a wiretap on the telephone of a Sikh Canadian in British Columbia.
There is clearly a powerful temptation to obtain the result wanted, whether it be a wiretap or a confession, by any means that will work when security forces are under pressure to do
their job effectively. Truth and justice can easily become casualties in the rush to show results.
I urge the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) to enquire carefully into the interrogation of Daljit Singh Sekhon and to ensure that proper procedures have been followed. The rights of all Canadians need the protection of the Canadian Government, especially when the hunt is on for terrorists.

Mr. Speaker, final deficit figures are now available for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1987. It is encouraging that, due to the policy of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) of fiscal restraint, the deficit was S30.6 billion, or $400 million less than forecast.
When this Government took control three years ago in 1984, the 1984-85 deficit was $38.3 billion and climbing rapidly because of the out of control spending policies of the former Liberal Government. Its irresponsible, reckless spending habits launched this country into awesome increases in the national debt through year after year increases in annual deficits.
Regrettably, the total accumulated national debt is now $280 billion, or $11,000 for every man, woman and child in the country. Almost 35 cents of every tax dollar collected is now required to pay the interest on this monstrous debt. Canadians should never forget, nor forgive the former Liberal Government for the enormity and tragic cost of its fiscal mismanagement. Our children and grandchildren will be paying the price for decades to come.

Mr. Speaker, in 1985 I originally proposed amendments to the Criminal Code to allow for the prosecution of war criminals, which found favour with the Deschenes Commission. I am pleased to compliment Canada's Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn), and all Parties in this House, on the quick passage of the War Crimes Bill.
The passage of the Bill does not, however, bring the process to an end. The Government must now show it is committed to using the new powers contained in the Bill to prosecute war criminals in Canada. In a sense, the term "war criminal" is somewhat of a misnomer because we are not talking in the


Oral Question
main about the killing of combatants in the course of a war but about the murder of innocents and the persecution of a race.
Exceptional crimes justify exceptional pursuit within the framework of our legal system. The Minister of Justice, having expressed his resolve on this issue, has no time to lose in bringing war criminals to justice. There is a new urgency in the search for war criminals, not out of vengeance but for the sake of remembrance. Remembrance remains a powerful tool, a censure against extremism. The Deschenes Commission has kept alive the flame of the memory of the victims of the Holocaust. Let us be sure its light of justice is not left to flicker out.

subtopic: REMOVAL OF RESTRICTIONS ON NATURAL GAS EXPORTS
REMOVAL OF RESTRICTIONS ON NATURAL GAS EXPORTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one of our major policies during the 1984 election campaign was reconciliation. We promised to end discriminatory practices such as the national energy policy. This Government ended the NEP. Crude oil can be sold at market prices. Unfair and unjust taxes were terminated.
This Government requested the National Energy Board to review the discriminatory restrictions on exporting natural gas. Last week's announcement by the NEB removing these restrictions is indeed welcome news in western Canada. It means greater exports, more jobs and more prosperity.
We have delivered on reconciliation.

subtopic: PLIGHT OF HOMELESS-CALL FOR INCREASED FUNDING
PLIGHT OF HOMELESS-CALL FOR INCREASED FUNDING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this week at the Ottawa Congress Centre the Canadian conference to observe the International Year of Shelter for the Homeless has brought together representatives of all levels of government, non-governmental organizations, and service agencies, to discuss solutions to the problems of homelessness in Canada and, indeed, around the world. I call upon the Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing, a major sponsor of this conference, to commit the Government to fund additional units for the hard-to-house in Canada as a substantial and meaningful contribution to the homeless in the country.
Also marking the International Year of Shelter for the Homeless, community-based groups from Ottawa, Montreal and other Canadian cities are assembling on Lebreton Flats to
remind the Government of Canada that the Flats once provided affordable housing, and that future redevelopment plans must include such housing.
I further call upon the Minister responsible for the National Capital Commission, which is the land-owner of Lebreton Flats, to commit the Government to providing land to cooperative and non-profit housing agencies to construct such housing as part of any redevelopment plan on the Flats.

subtopic: PLIGHT OF HOMELESS-CALL FOR INCREASED CANADIAN COMMITMENT
PLIGHT OF HOMELESS-CALL FOR INCREASED CANADIAN COMMITMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in 1983, when the Liberals were in power, a contribution of $300,000 was made to the International Year of Shelter for the Homeless. Canada took its role seriously and was the first largest contributor among the ranks of developed countries.
However, by mid-1986, 80 per cent of the pledges had originated in developing nations where, as we know, shelter requirements are most intense. Today the Canadian commitment must go beyond this International Year of Shelter for the Homeless. We must act as a beacon among industrialized nations in the quest for a solution to the homeless problem abroad and, indeed, at home.
I call upon the Government to recommit Canada to the resolution of homelessness in the world, and to present the appropriate measures to solve the problem at home. The Government must show as strong commitment in 1987 as the Liberals did in 1983. Instead, the Conservative Government has increased taxes for Canadians by $22 billion since taking power just three years ago, and it has neglected the homeless.

speakeroldname: Hon. James Kelleher (Solicitor General of Canada):

subsubtopic: ACCURACY OF AFFIDAVITS-REQUEST FOR MINISTER'S RESIGNATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I might just say by way of preamble that I find it interesting to hear the author of the CSIS legislation asking questions that result clearly from abuses for which that legislation he authored was responsible.


Oral Question
My question is directed to the Solicitor General. It concerns the most recent annual report of the Security Intelligence Review Committee which states:
We are informed that the Solicitor General makes sure, in reviewing warrant applications, that everything being sworn to is an ascertainable fact, not merely a conclusion the investigator has drawn from the facts, and he sends some applications back for amendment before he lets them go to the Federal Court.. . We welcome his vigilance.
In view of the suggestion that the Solicitor General himself is personally responsible for the accuracy of affidavits sworn in request for warrants, and having fired the Director of CSIS, does he not accept his responsibility for this deceitful warrant? If so, why does he not do the honourable thing and resign as Solicitor General?

speakeroldname: Hon. James Kelleher (Solicitor General of Canada):
subsubtopic: ACCURACY OF AFFIDAVITS-REQUEST FOR MINISTER'S RESIGNATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I have already pointed out to the House earlier and I will repeat again, the affidavit which supported this warrant was reviewed and sworn in June of 1985. Immediately upon it coming to this Solicitor General's attention, I initiated the actions of which I told the House. I think we and the Government have acted quickly, fairly and decisively in this matter.
I can assure the Hon. Member that it has been my practice since I became Solicitor General carefully to review and read each affidavit in support of an application for warrant that comes before me. It has always been my practice to discuss the warrant before signing it with the Director or the Acting Director in concert with other officers of CSIS.

Mr. Speaker, given the history of CSIS, it is a security agency which is clearly in a state of crisis and disarray. There have been problems with civilianization, with bilingualism, and with bungled investigations in the case of the Sikh situation. There have been fights with the RCMP, and targeting of individuals who should not have been targeted. There has been serious criticism by SIRC.
Why is the Minister afraid to allow Parliament to review comprehensively the actions of CSIS today? Why is he insisting we wait two more years for the review of an agency in disarray? In light of his refusal to allow Parliament to conduct this comprehensive review today, why on earth does he not resign? He is obviously not in control of the agency for which he is responsible.

speakeroldname: Hon. James Kelleher (Solicitor General of Canada):
speechtext:
With the greatest respect, Mr. Speaker, I do not share the opinion of the Hon. Member that CSIS is in a state of disarray. That is unfair to the Service. I think it is doing a commendable job, and that is contained in the latest SIRC report, parts of which he chose not to read.
The language issue is being dealt with decisively. An action plan is now ready and I hope to present it within the next few
weeks. The Osbaldeston committee is looking into the matters of counter-subversion and civilianization. I think the agency is alive and well. There are some minor problems and they are being dealt with.

speechtext:

subtopic: CRIMINAL CODE, FOOD AND DRUGS ACT AND NARCOTIC CONTROL ACT MEASURE TO AMEND

speechtext: The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Hnatyshyn that Bill C-61, an Act to amend the Criminal Code, the Food and Drugs Act and the Narcotic Control Act, be read the second time and referred to a Legislative Committee.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: CRIMINAL CODE, FOOD AND DRUGS ACT AND NARCOTIC CONTROL ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: When the House rose at one o'clock, the Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis) had the floor.

subtopic: CRIMINAL CODE, FOOD AND DRUGS ACT AND NARCOTIC CONTROL ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in concluding my remarks on Bill C-61, I was pointing out a major flaw in the Bill that I believe all Parties will want to change. While there are many flaws in Bill C-61, the New Democratic Party supports its principle. It will allow the Government to take serious steps toward eliminating drug abuse and drug trafficking in our country.
Of course, under the present legislation, drug traffickers can easily invest and use the banking system to launder money. While they may serve some time in prison, they can come out to resume their business with substantial amounts of income that they have invested in various ways, not only in Canada but throughout the world.
The major flaw in this legislation is that it does not encompass the banking and financial communities. Serious allegations have been made in the press in the last number of months about money from illicit drug trafficking finding its way into various deposits in Canadian financial institutions. There is no definite proof of this since the books are closed. The RCMP and other law enforcement agencies do not have access to those bank accounts, unlike the United States where financial institutions are required to report their deposits over a certain amount on a regular basis. As a matter of fact, they must report a number of items. This allows the law enforcement authorities in the United States to identify where drug money is being laundered through financial institutions.


We assumed that appropriate legislation reflecting that situation would be introduced. However, such is not the case. Bill C-61 does not include Canadian financial institutions as part of the monitoring system. When this matter goes before the appropriate legislative committee, I urge my honourable colleagues to consider using the experience in the United States, where drug rings have been smashed as a result of the information provided by the reporting systems of the American financial institutions.
While this might require some new responsibilities for banking personnel, as well as some systems for that accounting, I am convinced that if such a request was made of the Canadian Bankers' Association and the organizations of other financial institutions, they would co-operate. It would be in the best interest of Canada, particularly in terms of Canada's young people, if we could put a stop or at least inhibit the running of illicit drugs that presently occurs in our schools, colleges, universities, as well as on the streets of Canada.
If this legislation can be amended in that area, it would certainly have the support of New Democrats on the committee. I am sure it would also have the support of other political parties because stopping the traffic in illicit drugs on the streets of Canada surely is not a partisan issue but something all parliamentarians would endorse.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question which I already asked the Government in regard to its drug reform program and legislative changes. Would it not be a good idea to take into consideration as part of drug abuse the glue sniffing that goes on in many communities across this country?
In Winnipeg, at the City Hall level, we had a by-law for a short time regulating the sale of products which could be abused by youngsters. They were put behind the counter and the age level at which they could be purchased was restricted. This by-law had a positive effect in Winnipeg by reducing the abuse of products on which children could get high by sniffing which, of course, has a detrimental effect on their health and mental capacity.
I wonder if my colleague would not agree that it is a little strange that the Government, which is attacking drug abuse, is not at the same time taking the opportunity to amend federal laws which could reduce the abuse of products that children use to get high, thereby destroying their health?
The by-law which existed in Winnipeg was ruled ultra vires by the court in that it fell within federal jurisdiction. Would this not be a good area for initiative by the federal Government at this time?

subtopic: CRIMINAL CODE, FOOD AND DRUGS ACT AND NARCOTIC CONTROL ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my friend, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Keeper) makes a good suggestion, and it is not the first time he has made it. I recall that he suggested it on numerous occasions, both in public and private. He has put that question in committee and many times on the
Proceeds of Crime
floor of the House of Commons, trying to encourage the Government to take a variety of steps which would bring to an end that type of activity by young people, not only in Winnipeg but right across the country.
I can only imagine his level of frustration today when once again there is a missed opportunity. Here is an opportunity for the Government to take steps, to indicate in the introductory speeches by government Members how the Government plans to deal with this problem. But once again it has turned its back on something which is very serious. Perhaps we will have an opportunity during debate on this legislation, and more particularly during the work which will be done in the legislative committee, to raise the importance of taking fast action in this critical area.
I also think that when we deal with legislation such as Bill C-61, finding ways and means of legislating the reduction in the amount of illicit drugs sold, drug trafficking and the abuse of drugs, that we do not lose sight of the need to fight the reasons for drug abuse. I think all too often we get too caught up in the mechanics of legislation, in our role as legislators, trying to stem the tide, to fight the symptoms of a much deeper concern. We as responsible parliamentarians should ask the question, what is it that is driving our young people to sniff glue? What is it that drives our young people in high schools and, more unfortunately, in our elementary schools, to pursue drugs and get caught up in the dastardly web of drug abuse? What is it that exists in our society that causes people to require this particular outlet?

speechtext: This Government.

subtopic: CRIMINAL CODE, FOOD AND DRUGS ACT AND NARCOTIC CONTROL ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
My friend, the Hon. Member for Beaches (Mr. Young), perhaps not so humourously, says perhaps it is the Government's inaction on a whole number of fronts. You recall, Madam Speaker, the questions raised about illiteracy when the shocking facts recently came out in terms of the incredibly high level of illiteracy among Canadian adults. In some provinces it was in excess of 40 per cent of the adult population. We have tens of thousands, I must say even hundreds of thousands of Canadians in the workforce who are illiterate and, consequently, are the last hired and first fired. This is one of the fundamental problems which results in drug abuse. It provides an incentive for those who would exploit these people and, therefore, the illicit trafficking of drugs increases. Madam Speaker, I would also like to ask about the question raised this morning with respect to the Government spending $210 million on enforcement in the drug offence area and its failure to address the major problem of


Supreme Court Act
chemical addiction. I would like to ask the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis) for his comments on the failure of the Government to address the major problem of alcohol abuse.
I would like to outline a small area of which I know he is familiar, that is, the community of Bella Coola. An alcohol rehabiltation counsellor in that community is paid $12,000 a year, yet saves both the federal and provincial Governments hundreds of thousands of dollars a year by helping people with an alcohol problem. If it is a parent, the parent can go to work, and the family is assisted.
The Government saves thousands of dollars in health and social services. However, The federal Government will not pay those salaries for people to assist and treat alcoholics. In the community of Bella Coola one of the largest single causes of crime is abuse of alcohol. Everything else stems from it, from child abuse to murder, to assault, to impaired driving. Only $12,000 is the cost of an alcohol abuse counsellor. These alcohol abuse counsellors have a track record of saving hundreds of thousands of dollars.
I ask the opinion of the Hon. Member for Kamloops- Shuswap. Is the Government not being extremely short-sighted in dealing with the small end of the spectrum instead of contributing the resources of the people of Canada to the other problem areas? We are not begrudging the efforts made to curb the serious problem of drug abuse, drug trafficking and drug offences. However, we want money spent in the area of alcohol rehabilitation and treatment so we can realize the savings in human terms, in health terms and in financial terms for the people of Canada.

subtopic: CRIMINAL CODE, FOOD AND DRUGS ACT AND NARCOTIC CONTROL ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, once again, I appreciate the most thoughtful interjection of the Hon. Member for Comox-Powell River (Mr. Skelly) on this very critical issue. It is an issue of profound interest to us all. I think too often when it comes to requests for funding of facilities to treat the victims of alcohol and drug abuse we do not have the money to spend-the treasury is bare. Spending in these areas, while it is certainly a concern, is not necessarily a high priority. I think the word "priority" itself betrays a particular attitude. I think we have to see money used to move people away from a dependency on chemicals. Money used to move people away from a reliance on alcohol and drugs is not money spent, but money invested. That money, when it saves a young man or woman, will result in vast savings because they will not spend their time in centres of care later on or cause other problems in terms of death on our highways and so on.
I think we have to see this as an investment in our future in terms of preventive action. It is an non-partisan issue. I will use as an example the non-partisan way in which this ought to be treated. There are communities around the country, as we stand here, taking the initiative to open up treatment centres for those people who are caught up in the web of chemical dependencies. I do not have to refer to any other place than the community of Logan Lake in western Canada. People such as
my colleague, the Hon. Member for Cariboo-Chilcotin (Mr. Greenaway), myself and others are working hard to obtain the necessary financial support to assist people in that part of western Canada so that they can be treated for their dependency on chemicals of one kind or other. I am hopeful that as this Bill moves on to the legislative committee stage, we will be taking off our partisan hats and working to obtain the necessary changes and, of course, in the long term, the necessary funding, to bring drug and alcohol abuse in Canada to an end.

speakeroldname: Hon. Ray Hnatyshyn (Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
that Bill C-53, an Act to amend the Supreme Court Act and to amend various other Acts in consequence thereof, be read a second time and referred to a legislative committee.
He said: Madam Speaker, I am pleased to rise to speak briefly on this important legislation. Bill C-53 is a Bill to amend the Supreme Court Act and to amend various other Acts in consequence thereof. The aim of the Bill, while simple, is of considerable importance to the administration of justice in Canada. It is to alter the procedure for appeals to the Supreme Court of Canada so as to ensure that the court can continue deciding issues of fundamental national importance in an effective and timely manner.
The considerable increase in recent years in the number of cases heard by the court, particularly appeals based on the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, has underlined the fact that the court's time is a limited resource. A glance at a


Canadian newspaper on almost any given day will show the fundamental important questions that the court must decide. The amendments proposed in this Bill are necessary if the court is to continue dealing effectively with the growing number of cases referred to it. Without such amendments the court is increasingly likely to find itself unable to decide some of the important legal and constitutional issues of our time.
The Bill proposes six basic amendments. I would like to summarize them. First, the Bill provides that applications for leave to appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada in both civil and criminal matters may be determined on written submissions by the parties, if it is clear from such written submissions that an oral hearing is not warranted.
This amendment is designed to allow the court to make decisions on applications for leave to appeal without it being necessary to hold an oral hearing in cases where it is clear from the written submissions that the application should be granted or that it should be dismissed. At present, all applications for leave to appeal are heard by a three-member panel of the court. I should point out that 400 to 500 applications for leave are brought each year. The court grants leave to appeal in no more than 20 per cent to 30 per cent of these cases. Pursuant to the provisions of this Bill, if the court dispenses with even a small percentage of oral hearings, a substantial saving in time could be accomplished. The discretion will rest with the court to determine whether an oral hearing is warranted or not pursuant to the provisions of the Bill. Nothing in the Bill precludes the court from ordering an oral hearing where such is warranted.
Second, in order to allow the Supreme Court to handle its proceedings more effectively the Bill provides that the court may deliver a judgment either in open court or, as is the case with many courts across the land, by depositing a copy with the Registrar. This amendment will give the court the same discretion to deliver a judgment by depositing it with the Registrar, which is something that all provincial courts of appeal now do. I think it applies to all courts across the country.
An Member opposite is shaking his head.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The Member opposite has probably not appeared in every court of appeal across the land, either as a lawyer or as an accused. I will accept his acknowledgement that he does not know exactly the procedure in all cases.
The Supreme Court Act presently requires that judgments be delivered in open court and that the majority of the judges who presided at the hearing of the appeal be present for the delivery of that judgment. Obviously, this involves the time of members of the court, as well as the time and expense of counsel attending the court to receive the judgment. In all reason the court should have the discretion to determine whether the rendering of judgment in open court is necessary or appropriate.
Supreme Court Act
Third, the Bill will give to the Supreme Court the authority to assign counsel to act on behalf of an unrepresented accused. Under this amendment, the Attorney General involved will bear the cost where legal aid is not granted to the accused. Furthermore, the fees of counsel may be taxed by the Registrar of the court. This proposal extends to the Supreme Court of Canada an authority that has already been given to the provincial courts of appeal by Section 611 of the Criminal Code of Canada.
In recent years the number of inmates appearing before the Supreme Court to conduct their own appeals has been increasing. Real concerns have been raised about the ability of inmates to present legal arguments. Furthermore, in those cases where the unrepresented inmate does not appear, Crown counsel argues both for the appellant inmate and the respondent Crown. Bill C-53 responds to these concerns regarding fairness by providing legislative authority for the provision of counsel to ensure that important questions are fully and thoroughly argued.
Fourth, since all appeals to the court involve questions of law, and given the amendment to permit the assignment of counsel to unrepresented accused, the Bill provides that an appellant who is in custody and who is respresented by counsel will not be entitled as of right to be present at an appeal or any preliminary or incidental proceeding. However, provision is made for the rules of court to allow attendance by inmates and for the court or a judge thereof to grant leave for the inmate to attend. This change to the Act gives the Supreme Court of Canada the same discretion as is presently available to courts of appeal pursuant to Section 615(2) of the Criminal Code of Canada.
Fifth, the Bill proposes that certain appeals as of right provided for in the Criminal Code and other statutes be abolished. Under the proposal an appellant who can now appeal to the Supreme Court as of right would thus henceforth first have to obtain leave to appeal from the court. I have received certain representations making known to me concerns with this particular element of the Bill. After careful consideration I have decided that I will bring forward an amendment to preserve the present practice regarding appeals as of right. I will bring those forward at the time that this Bill is considered in committee.
Finally, in order to overcome the present problems with the time limits for bringing an appeal, the Bill proposes amendments to make the time limits for bringing an appeal and for filing an application for leave to appeal more reasonable and practical. The time limits for obtaining leave to appeal and bringing an appeal in a criminal matter are difficult to meet. For instance, under Section 618 of the Criminal Code an appellant is given 21 days to bring an application for leave to appeal and to obtain the leave of the court. Because of the difficulty in meeting this time period, applications for an extension of the time period are routinely brought and granted.


Supreme Court Act
In addition to this problem, the fact that different time periods are applicable to criminal and civil matters causes unnecessary difficulties and confusion. Bill C-53 standardizes the time periods applicable to both civil and criminal matters and places them within one statute, that is, the Supreme Court Act.
In conclusion, Bill C-53 is intended to ensure that our Supreme Court will retain its ability to deal effectively with questions of fundamental national importance while ensuring fairness.
1 should like to draw to the attention of all Hon. Members the fact that the Canadian Bar Association has called for reform. In 1985, the Canadian Bar Association, at its annual meeting in Halifax, approved a resolution which called for all applications for leave to appeal, criminal and civil, to be determined by the Supreme Court of Canada on written submissions unless an oral hearing was ordered. The Bar recognized the need to improve accessibility for questions of national importance.
I should like to refer to the Canadian Bar Association Committee's report under the chairmanship of Mr. Claude R. Thomson. In part page 55 reads:
Bill C-53, first reading, May 4, 1987, by clause 4, would authorize the Court to dispense with an oral hearing in those cases where "it is clear from the written material" that the criteria for leave are, or are not, satisfied. In all other cases, the present practice of an oral hearing would continue.
The Committee endorses the change proposed by Bill C-53. The Bill preserves the general principle that there ought to be an oral hearing for every application for which an oral hearing could be useful. But it dispenses with an oral hearing in those cases where the hearing would be a waste of the Court's time.
Not only will the Bill C-53 proposal save hearing time for the Court, it will spare the parties much of the cost of an application for leave-the Committee is satisfied that Bill C-53 is a desirable reform that ought to be proceeded with now.
I think lawyers and Hon. Members interested in the operation of our courts, particularly the Supreme Court of Canada, would agree that we should take steps as quickly as possible to allow the court to deal with and to spend the time on substantive issues, particularly with the impact of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms on the Supreme Court and the additional onus it places upon the court to give considered views in respect of very important issues.
I would say that this Bill is a first initiative on the part of the Government to help the court to husband its time and to allow it to direct its attention to important national legal issues facing it.
I will be glad to discuss in committee further details in respect of this matter. However, I simply wanted to say at this time that there has been much consideration of a wide range of issues respecting what we might do in terms of our court system in order to ensure that these matters are dealt with by the court on a proper and timely basis.
I am very much aware of my obligations as Minister of Justice-and they are obligations of those of us in the House- to consider what can be done to facilitate the court system, to ensure that things go through expeditiously at a minimum amount of cost, and to ensure that the people of Canada are well served by the highest court in the land.
We are well served by the Supreme Court of Canada. All Hon. Members would share the view that the men and women of that court have displayed great dedication, ability, and competence. They are a credit to us. It is a central institution of Canada. I know I reflect the views of all Hon. Members of the House when I pay tribute to the justices of the Supreme Court of Canada. They have a Canadian perspective. They have dealt with the laws of our lands in a very learned and Canadian way. I think these are high compliments to the court, and I think these views would be shared by all Members of the House.
I ask Hon. Members to support these amendments so that we can all share in working toward an improvement of the system to ensure that the Supreme Court of Canada in fact has the ability to serve the best interests of all Canadians.

Madam Speaker, over the years Parliament has done very little to improve the life of the Supreme Court of Canada. In fact, it has been the opposite. We have, with an ever increasing frequency, passed laws of increasing sophistication and complexity. We have amended our Constitution and have proposed to re-amend it. The burden faced by the Supreme Court of Canada, compared with the burden at any period in the past, can only be described in comparative terms as overwhelming.
Therefore, when a thoughtful and serious collection of improvements is put forward, as it is before the House now, to improve the efficiency of the court in some ways without purportedly taking anything away from its fairness, I think we must take it very seriously and do everything we can in this place to facilitate the work of the court.
When I talk about efficiency and fairness, I think account has to be had, as the Minister indicated, of the cost of the system of justice and ways in which that cost can be kept to a minimum and can be reduced. I think those principles have animated the amendments which are before us. While I want to express some reservations about them, I want to say also that it is a timely Bill. It is one that I suggest on behalf of the Official Opposition will be given expeditious treatment. We look forward to hearing from the Minister. In dealing with the recommendations of the Canadian Bar Association, we ought to be open to the Bar if it wants to appear before us. I have seen the Claude Thomson report. I think it is excellent and may in fact obviate even the necessity of having the Canadian Bar Association appear before us.
It must be said, however, that something is being lost from the point of view of the citizen in what we are doing today-


and if it is necessary that it be lost, it is nonetheless regrettable-that is, the ancient right, which few countries have been able to preserve but which we have preserved to this day, of getting a hearing on a request for leave to appeal. I know that some concern has been expressed across the country about this being lost. When we look at the amount of work involved in maintaining that ancient right, we must recognize that perhaps its time has come.
1 should like to see the statistics-I am sure the Minister will have them-and to see the evidence. I am looking forward to deciding whether we can hold up our heads and go back to our constituents to tell them that a great historic right has been taken away from them in the interest of ensuring that the court has the time to consider properly the cases which merit real consideration.
The Minister referred to his plan to introduce amendments of his own to the fifth amendment proposed in the Bill. 1 will not take time to talk about it; I am glad it is being done. It is a reasonable response, but of course I should like to see the amendments he is proposing.
Finally, I want to say a word about the provision with which I had some experience as Solicitor General when inmates had to be brought to the Supreme Court of Canada from wherever they were in the country in connection with even very peripheral aspects relating to their cases before the Supreme Court of Canada. Ordinary citizens in the same situation could ill afford to come to Ottawa to be present for matters which were truly peripheral by any definition of the word. Yet, because of the existing Act, we had the practice of bringing them to the nation's capital at great expense and, in some cases, at considerable danger to themselves or to others, when we were talking about very violent criminals whose appeals were the issues before the Supreme Court of Canada.
Taxpayers should welcome this particular amendment because it takes nothing substantial away from the offender. It puts him more or less in the same position as the ordinary citizen in deciding whether he can afford to follow his lawyer to the nation's capital to make the case on a relatively minor aspect of his cause before the Supreme Court of Canada.
We will not, in the Official Opposition, rubber-stamp the Bill. We recognize all of the pressures that make it desirable at this time for the Supreme Court of Canada to undertake this amount of streamlining, which I hope we will find at the end of our investigation takes nothing away from fairness toward the applicants who are seeking the attention of the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court of Canada is an ornament of Canadian society. One can see by the controversy around the Meech Lake proposals that affect the composition of the Supreme Court of Canada how precious that institution is to Canadians and how much they want it to work and work well.
I will not use this occasion to make comments about the impact of the Meech Lake Accord on the Supreme Court of
Supreme Court Act
Canada, but I think it was significant that so many Canadians responded emotionally and with a sense of patriotism to measures that might adversely affect the institution.
The Supreme Court has an ever more important role to play in adjudicating claims between the provincial level of government and the federal level. It also has this very important responsibility under the Charter of adjudicating the limits of government, where it is that a citizen can stand and not have his or her rights or privacy invaded any further by the state. I look forward to the consideration of this Bill in committee, and I hope we will be able to undertake it very soon.

Madam Speaker, at the outset of my remarks on Bill C-53 1 want to join in the remarks and the tributes made by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn) and the Hon. Member for York Centre (Mr. Kaplan), the Justice spokesperson for his Party, to the Supreme Court of Canada.

There is no doubt that the men and women who sit on the Supreme Court of Canada serve with high distinction on the highest court in this country. We are very pleased that the Government has appointed two women to this most important tribunal. However, I hope that, in the very near future, at least half the members of this court will be women.

Traditionally, the Supreme Court of Canada has appointed on a non-partisan basis the most outstanding jurists from across Canada, obviously in conjuction with the provisions governing the Supreme Court of Canada. We in this Party, however, certainly join in acknowledging the outstanding contribution that has been made historically and is being made today by the Supreme Court of Canada. It is also important to note that the role of the Supreme Court of Canada today has been significantly enhanced as a result of the adoption in Canada of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. It is now up to the Supreme Court of Canada ultimately to decide the full meaning of the provisions of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, to decide, for example, what are the limits on the rights and freedoms set out in the Charter which are demonstrably justifiable in a free and democratic society. 1 would like to be able to say as well that the Supreme Court of Canada on these questions of fundamental civil liberties and human rights is, in fact, the final voice. It is there in a position to defend the rights of minorities against the occasional tyranny of the majority. I very much regret, however, as does my Party that that is not the case.
As a result of the inclusion of the so-called override provision in the Charter of Rights, Section 33, the most basic, fundamental and precious human rights and freedoms in Canada can be wiped out at the stroke of a legislative pen. If a simple majority, and I emphasize a simple majority, of parliamentarians at the federal level or at the provincial level disagree with a decision of the highest court of the land, the


Supreme Court Act
Supreme Court of Canada can overturn that decision merely by a majority vote.
We in this Party believe profoundly that this provision of the Charter of Rights, Section 33, fundamentally undermines that commitment to equality, to justice and to civil liberties which is so essential. We strongly urge the Government as a top priority to take the necessary steps to meet with its provincial counterparts, in other words, for the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) to meet with the First Ministers and do whatever he can to improve Section 33 of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. The price that was paid for adoption is one that could potentially seriously threaten civil liberties.
We believe that the role of the Supreme Court is important not only in the area of criminal and civil appeals but in particular in putting flesh and substance on the Charter of Rights, explaining to Canadians clearly what is meant and being prepared, when necessary, to act as a check on Governments which override those fundamental provisions in the Charter of Rights. My colleague from York Centre, the Justice spokesperson for the Liberal Party, indicated that he believes the legislation with which we are now dealing is a thoughtful and serious piece of legislation, as he put it. Fie said, and he is absolutely right, that this is one of the first pieces of legislation to come before this House to deal in any substantive way with the Supreme Court for many years. I want to disagree very strongly with my colleague's from York Centre characterization of this legislation as thoughtful and serious. Rather, this legislation, were it to be adopted by this House, would instead constitute a fundamental erosion of some very precious and important rights of Canadian men and women. I will explain why I believe that to be the case, why I believe that this legislation is wrong in principle, and why we in the New Democratic Party are not prepared to support the legislation as it is presently worded.
We all understand the sense of frustration and at times of annoyance perhaps that the Supreme Court of Canada feels at a work-load that is clearly a very heavy work-load. Under the existing provisions of the Supreme Court Act individuals are entitled to an oral hearing on an application of leave to appeal. As well, the discretion of the court to decide for itself which cases it wishes to hear is to some extent fettered. Let me suggest that when one examines the history of these provisions and looks at why it is, with respect to certain appeals, that the appeal goes as a right, it would be a profound mistake, a tragic mistake and a move backwards for this Parliament to deny those appeals as a right.
There are certainly provisions in the legislation with which we have no quarrel. There are provisions that would allow the Supreme Court of Canada to deliver judgment by depositing a judgment with the Registrar. As those lawyers who practise before the court are well aware, at the present time there are certain judgment days, something like 12 or more each year. During those judgment days lawyers queue up, the court is jammed with people and the judgments are handed down one after the other.
The present provisions of the Supreme Court Act require that judgments be delivered in open court. There is a certain amount of drama and excitement that attends to the handing down of judgments in open court. In addition to this particular provision, a majority of the judges who preside at the hearing of an appeal must be present for the delivery of the judgment. Practically speaking, the entire Supreme Court is present for the handing down of judgments or, in any event, a substantial majority of Members. In the case of provincial courts of appeal, however, they are entitled to deliver judgments either in open court or by depositing them with the Registrar. The amendment to the Supreme Court Act which would give to the highest court in the land the same discretion to deliver judgment by deposit that the courts of appeal already enjoy is certainly one that we support and recognize will go some way towards saving the time of that very important court.
The next major clause of the Bill would provide that the court determine applications for leave to appeal on the written submissions of the parties unless it orders an oral hearing. It would allow the court to fix the time within which an oral hearing must be held and would provide for quorum for applications for leave to appeal.
Superficially, perhaps, this particular amendment is somewhat attractive. The case-load of the Supreme Court of Canada is a very heavy one. Indeed, it is growing each year. However, I suggest that this particular provision is one that we will want to examine very carefully in committee. We will want to hear evidence from witnesses before agreeing to this provision.
Yes, it is true that there may be applications for leave to appeal which, in the words of the clause, make it clear from the written material that the application does not come within the provisions of Section 41 and therefore does not warrant an oral hearing. There may similarly be other applications which, quite obviously, given the significance and importance of the issues raised in the appeal, do come within those provisions and thus should give rise almost as a right to an appeal.
We must ask ourselves what we are sacrificing in achieving these objectives of speed and of cutting down on the number of oral hearings on leave to appeal. I believe that the price we are paying is one which may very well be too high. I will certainly want to hear evidence on this question in the legislative committee.
Let us take a moment to examine some of the arguments, and quite compelling ones, that have been raised against this particular provision. There can be no substitute for the court itself hearing from counsel rather than pouring over page after page of written material. Frequently a point that can be made effectively in an oral hearing simply cannot be made as effectively in writing. The skills of advocacy are often brought to bear in a far more effective way at a direct, oral hearing


rather than at one in which judges simply review written material.
Yes, it is true that in some cases these hearings result in additional expense and some additional delay, but the reality as well is that the court has recently moved to a system of hearings by remote video. This has occurred in areas in British Columbia, and if it is not already happening in Newfoundland and the Maritime Provinces, I am sure it will be happening there in the near future as well. Those hearings have in fact proven to be very effective.
The Supreme Court has shown that it is able to adapt modern technology in a way that will assist it in providing hearings on leave to appeal and in cutting down the costs to litigants. However, I believe it is important that counsel should be in a position to present his or her argument cogently and clearly in an oral way at an oral hearing and not simply by means of written material.
There is another problem with this as well. There is a danger that judges will simply delegate the reading of motion papers on applications for leave to appeal to their clerks. There is no question whatsoever that this is already happening in the Supreme Court of the United States. I am not suggesting that clerks are not quite able to assist the judiciary in this important task, but the fact is that at the end of the day, it is the judges' job and responsibility. Surely a litigant who goes to the highest court of the land is entitled to know that his or her motion for leave was determined by the judge himself or herself and not by one of the judge's clerks.
I think we must also look ahead to the implications of this amendment on possible changes of a more fundamental nature to hearings before the Supreme Court of Canada. I am afraid that if we accept this clause, we will next hear arguments that appeals themselves should be limited. This in effect will turn appeals into paper wars. This has happened already in the Supreme Court of the United States where in even the most significant and important cases, oral argument is limited to 30 minutes for each side. In the United States, it is the consideration of written briefs by judges and clerks that plays the most important role in the final decision.
Obviously, given the population of the United States which is 10 times that of Canada and the fact that the American court is the same size as the Canadian court, perhaps it has been driven to that expedient. However, in our country, I suggest that this cannot be justified. I am concerned that were we to adopt the proposal which is presently before the House, it could lead to pressure for limitations on the actual appeal hearings as well.
Thomas Berger, a distinguished lawyer who also served on the Supreme Court of British Columbia for 11 years, I believe, has seen this question from both sides. As he has stated:
To reduce the whole matter to paper seems to me to downgrade the role of
advocacy; this is not in keeping with the traditions of our bar.
It is not simply that this contributes to the openness of the justice system at
the very highest level; my argument is that it enables the court better to
Supreme Court Act
understand the exact question that is before it. This contributes to better
decision making.
I believe that Thomas Berger is absolutely right. When this Bill does go to committee, it will be up to the Government to bring forward compelling arguments indicating why we should not accept the counsel of Thomas Berger, given his perspective as counsel and as a distinguished former member of the judiciary. It should allow those who are seeking leave to appeal at the highest court of the land the opportunity to be heard orally on that application.
What are the other major provisions of the legislation? There are a couple of other provisions with respect to time limits for bringing appeals and applications for leave to appeal before the Supreme Court of Canada. Once again, we certainly have no objection to this. This is a provision that is overdue and in effect would attempt to make more uniform the time periods for appeal, particularly in criminal and civil matters. This amendment responds to those problems, and we support it.
There are provisions as well with respect to the attendance by inmates before the Supreme Court of Canada. Given the other new provision which would allow for the authority to assign counsel explicitly to the Supreme Court of Canada, it may very well be that these are provisions which can be supported as well. We will certainly want to hear further evidence on that point.
At the present time, while the rules of the Supreme Court of Canada allow for the appointment of counsel to act on behalf of an accused appearing before the court, that is not explicitly set out in the Supreme Court of Canada Act. We agree that when appearing before the highest court of the land which deals with such important and serious questions as come before it, no one should be denied access to the court because of inability to afford counsel. Once again, we welcome the provision that explicitly allows the court to appoint counsel.
Those are the major provisions of the legislation, save and except one other clause which I suggest is profoundly wrong and which would deny Canadians who are seeking justice, fairness and equity from the highest court of the land an opportunity to be heard when they are fully entitled to that right to be so heard. I was surprised to hear the Justice spokesman for the Liberal Party describing this legislation as thoughtful and serious while not raising any concern whatsoever about a provision in this Bill which would profoundly and seriously change the existing rights of appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada. It is one thing to say Canadians will no longer have the automatic right to an oral hearing before the Supreme Court of Canada. We have serious questions about that, but they can be studied in committee. It is something else to examine with care some of the procedural changes which, in most cases, are long overdue to facilitate the work of the Supreme Court of Canada. However, that part of this Bill which would fundamentally change the right of Canadians to appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada in certain circumstances, which I will set out, we in this Party totally reject. We


Supreme Court Act
say it is wrong in principle and fundamentally undermines this legislation. For that reason we cannot possibly support this Bill on second reading.
Clauses 11 through 13 would abolish the right to appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada in two particular circumstances. First, when there has been a dissent before the Court of Appeal and, second, when a person has been acquitted of an indictable offence and the acquittal has been set aside by the Court of Appeal. These rights have been fought for by Canadians. Indeed, they have been at the corner-stone of the Canadian system of justice. My colleague from St. John's East, a very distinguished barrister in the Province of Newfoundland, will be commenting further with respect to these provisions.
The right of appeal in these circumstances has existed for a very important reason. We presume that provincial Court of Appeal judges are respected, knowledgeable and outstanding jurists. If one of those judges should disagree with his or her colleagues on an appeal, surely it is not good enough to say that the litigant should simply accept the fact that there is a difference of opinion and go no further. You can imagine the situation in which an individual is before the court seeking justice. He or she has persuaded a judge that there is a foundation to the appeal, only to be told that they can go no further or that they must seek the discretion of the Supreme Court of Canada before they can go any further.
There are many examples of the importance of this provision. One of the most recent is the appeal of Colin Thatcher, the former Saskatchewan politician now serving a life sentence for the first degree murder of his wife. When he appealed, four of the five judges on the Saskatchewan Court of Appeal dismissed it. One member of the court, however, was prepared to grant his appeal. It would have been profoundly wrong to say to him, or indeed any other litigant, that he has no right to seek the opinion of the highest court of the land when one of the judges at the appeal court level indicated dissent.
That brings me to another point. In many cases these appeals will go in circumstances in which an individual has been convicted of murder. Parliament has decreed that there is to be a 25-year minimum sentence before one can even be considered for parole. That was the price paid for the abolition of capital punishment in 1976. Many of us would argue that the price was very high, indeed, quite likely too high. That being said, surely an individual who faces the possibility of 25 years behind bars before even being eligible for parole, an individual who persuades an appellant court judge of the merits of that appeal, is entitled, before being locked up, to have it considered by the Supreme Court of Canada.
Similarly with respect to circumstances in which there has been an acquittal set aside by a provincial Court of Appeal. We all remember the profound injustice with respect to Dr. Henry Morgentaler. The amendment brought in by Ron
Basford, then Minister of Justice, at the strong urging of my predecessor as Justice critic, Stuart Leggatt, came too late for Henry Morgentaler. He quite unjustly served time in prison because, even though he had been acquitted by a jury of his peers, the Court of Appeal overturned the acquittal. That was a serious injustice and Parliament ruled that individuals would have the right to an automatic appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada in those circumstances. I suggest that in seeking to withdraw that right, the Government is taking a serious step backwards and diminishing the quality of justice in this country. We vigorously protest this provision in the Bill.
I was pleased to hear the undertaking of the Minister that he intends to support an amendment to delete those odious provisions. I made strong representations to the Minister on this point. I indicated that I intend to propose an amendment to delete this provision and I welcome his agreement to support my amendment and agree to the deletion of this very backward and regressive provision of the legislation.
In conclusion, while we in the NDP recognize that changes must be made, clearly we do not accept the Bill as worded. We must deal with the legislation before us, not with promises by the Minister for changes in committee. As it now stands, the Bill is so fundamentally flawed and would deny significant and important rights, that we in this Party will be voting against it on second reading.

Madam Speaker, I wish to follow the lead of other speakers in this debate in commending the Supreme Court of Canada for its great work and to acknowledge that it has the respect of all parts of the country for not only maintaining an appropriate balance between the laws of this country but for acting with great deliberation in making known and resolving major issues of not only constitutional but civil and criminal law. We all recognize the extent of their work-load and the fact that it has increased very dramatically in the last several years as a result of the introduction and passage of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. We see the need for and welcome certain measures which would make their work easier and take away some aspects of that work which appear to be unnecessary. I would like to look at all aspects of the Act to determine whether it will accomplish that without damaging the fundamental rights of Canadians.
There is, for example, a restriction on oral hearings or permission to restrict oral hearings on leave to appeal. My information is that oral hearings on leave to appeal applications take perhaps 12 days a year of court time. This may be a long period of time but it is not a great period of time. A similar amount of time is used in the delivery of judgments.
I believe, as do my colleague and many barristers across the country, that the oral hearing is a very important tool of the advocate, particularly in appeals before the Supreme Court of Canada. If the Supreme Court of Canada were predisposed,


based on written material presented to it, to grant leave to appeal, time could be saved by dispensing with the oral hearing. Such a measure would speed up proceedings and save the time of the judges of the Supreme Court which could more properly and fruitfully be spent dealing with the weighty matters before them.
Efowever, the provision of an oral hearing is of very great importance. As an advocate who has appeared before many courts, including the Supreme Court of Canada on a leave application, I attest to the value of an oral presentation. I myself have been convinced by oral presentations of advocates in cases where I was not persuaded by written material.
This Bill also contains the procedure for the assignment of counsel. This can be done under the existing rules, but we are told it is not done very often. We would look forward to it being done more often and the inclusion of it in the Act may result in some improvement. Elowever, it is really window dressing as the court already has the right to assign counsel when necessary.
There is also the provision for the delivery of judgments in written form by deposit in the registry instead of waiting for a judgment day, which sounds rather formidable. Some very important and weighty cases of great national significance may well benefit from the learned judges of the Supreme Court of Canada assembling together and making a verbal judgment.
However, in many cases the filing of a judgment, as is done in the provincial courts of appeal, would be perfectly adequate and may result in judgments being handed down more quickly. In fact, I know it would because quite often judgments are ready but cannot be delivered until the next judgment day. In matters of great national importance which affect the Constitution or more than just the litigants and establish very serious principles, the court may well prefer to read the judgments from the court itself.
There are a number of things in this Bill which, with a few amendments, could provide for the streamlining of court activity, save the court some time, and enable the work of the judges and the court to be conducted in a more fruitful way. We would support that sort of thing, but cannot support legislation which contains very serious regressive steps in terms of justice. The most significant are the removal of the automatic right of appeal in two cases, the first where there has been dissent in the provincial court of appeal, and the other where there has been acquittal by a jury.
The right of appeal, when there has been assent at the provincial court level, is, I believe, designed to provide uniformity in our laws across the country. A learned trial judge of the court of appeal of a province dissents from his colleagues when there is a serious divergence of opinion on a matter of great importance, a matter which may well be before the courts of other provinces in other ways.
Supreme Court Act
Two of three judges in a Newfoundland court may decide a particular question one way while two of three judges in the Province of Ontario may decide the question in another way. The purpose of having automatic appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada is to provide uniformity of laws across the country. We cannot have one criminal law for Newfoundland, another for Ontario and another for British Columbia. The law must be uniform across the country in terms of its interpretation and application. That fundamental change is thrown into this legislation under the guise of streamlining matters at the Supreme Court level.
The second exception which is more fundamental with regard to rights is with regard to acquittals by a jury when the provincial court of appeal has overthrown an acquittal and sent it back for a new trial. This is a matter of great fundamental importance which involves more than a change in procedure at the Supreme Court level. This is a matter of fundamental justice with regard to the approach to jury trials in this country.
We have adopted the centuries-old institution of the jury trial from the British legal tradition. In Britain if one is acquitted by a jury of one's peers chosen to hear the case, there is no appeal by the Crown allowed; In preserving the liberty of the subject and attempting to bring to justice someone who has committed a crime the state has only one opportunity to present the case properly.
In this country the Crown has the right of appeal from such an acquittal. A person acquitted by a jury of his peers is tried again if the Court of Appeal of a province decides that there has been a technical error in a case. My colleague, the Hon. Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson), has referred to the Morgentaler amendment as it has become known. Until that amendment, we had an even more fundamental problem in our country. The Court of Appeal could substitute a verdict of guilty after an individual had been acquitted by a jury of his peers. Thankfully, that amendment has removed that diminution of the great jury system.
The institution of the jury is one of the great preserves of the liberty of the subject. It has been said that the institution of the jury preserves the liberty of the subject sometimes in the face of the tyranny of the state. It is such a fundamental institution in our society that it would be a backward step from the progress that has been made to remove the automatic right of an individual to go to the Supreme Court of Canada to have an appeal heard when his acquittal by a jury has been repealed by a Court of Appeal as a result of a technicality.
It would be a backward step for us, after having passed an amendment which prevented the acquittal by a jury from being reversed by a Court of Appeal. That right of appeal to the Supreme Court upholds the institution of the jury at least to some extent. I and my Party would prefer to see the jury system be given the respect that it has been given in Britain so


Patens Extension (Aspartame) Act
that there would be no appeal at all. We support the institution of the jury in which its unanimous finding of acquittal is the end of the matter. At least, the current automatic right of appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada is some protection. Its removal is a fundamental change in our law and ought not to be part of any Bill that is purported to streamline the operations of court.
I understand that we have an undertaking from the Minister that there will be a response to amendments of this nature at committee level. I am pleased to hear that. Legislation with this fundamental flaw should not be before the House for second reading.
I am sympathetic to the importance of streamlining matters because the Supreme Court of Canada is overloaded with appeals. However, perhaps if the Government did not introduce some highly questionable Bills before the House, such as Bill C-84, there would not be so many appeals before the Supreme Court of Canada in an attempt to sort out the mistakes. In terms of procedure, I support the Government's measures to make it easier for the Supreme Court of Canada. However, I cannot and will not support in principle a Bill which has three fundamental flaws that affect the rights of Canadians under the guise of procedural changes.
