that Bill S-5, an Act to amend and consolidate the laws prohibiting marriage between related persons, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.
He said: Madam Speaker, I am very pleased to be able to say a few words on this Bill, which, as you know, originated in the other place, as it is referred to in this Chamber. It concerns the laws with respect to the capacity to marry.
When the British North America Act was passed in 1867, Parliament was given exclusive jurisdiction to legislate with respect to marriage and divorce and, more specifically, with respect to the capacity to marry. The provinces are involved in this area as well inasmuch as they have exclusive jurisdiction with respect to the solemnization of marriage. It is Parliament's prerogative to legislate in this particular area and it is on that basis that this Bill is presently before Parliament.
I believe it would be prudent at this point for Members of the House to reflect on some of the historical background to the question of prohibited degrees of marriage. It is, I would guess, one of the oldest areas of law still in effect in this country. A look at the historical aspects is especially important because although there are certain legal questions and arguments to consider, consideration of social ideals and norms that have developed throughout our history is important.
Our laws with respect to prohibited degrees of marriage, and the state's involvement in this area, goes back to Biblical times. In fact there are references in the Old Testament, the Book of Leviticus, Chapter 18, indicating what person another person could or could not marry.
As well, from the earliest times of Christianity and the involvement of the Christian Church with marriage, along with the solemnization of marriage conducted by the church, several norms grew up which indicated which related or nonrelated person, a person related, as we say in the legal profession, by consanguinity or affinity, someone could or could not marry. As the years went on, the Christian Church at various stages in its history, expanded or contracted the list according to the times. For instance, at one point in canon law one was prohibited from marrying a person within the seventh degree. I have not quite figured that out. I think it would be one's third
Marriage Prohibited Degrees Act
or fourth cousin. The present law in Canada originates from about the time of the so-called Reformation. At that time in the event of the church's history, Henry VIII and his Ministers set out a number of specific prohibitions. I suppose he is one monarch who had plenty to do with the subject of marriage, so it is somewhat appropriate he lend his hand to the statutory provisions. In 1563, a table of prohibited degrees was implemented in England. The table listed all the possible relationships up to and including the third degree, arising out of either blood or marriage, that would be prohibited. This table eventually found its way into the Anglican Book of Common Prayer. Eventually, the table was utilized by the ecclesiastical courts of England in annulment actions. Finally, the Lord Lyndhurst Act of 1835 indicated, among other things: "All marriages which shall hereafter be celebrated between persons within the prohibited degrees of consanguinity or affinity shall be absolutely null and void to all intents and purposes whatsoever". Such became the law of England in 1835. It was this law that was adopted by the common law jurisdictions of Canada and was then subsequently assumed, as I indicated, by the federal Government in 1867.
I should say that the laws were not exactly the same between the colonies and the provinces within the common law jurisdiction, but fortunately, they were very close to each other and, fortunately, as well, a civil law jurisdiction in Canada, namely, the Province of Quebec, had adopted laws that were essentially the same as its common law counterparts.
With the jurisdiction having passed to the federal Government in 1867, Parliament at various times tried its hand at the subject of the capacity to marry. In 1882, Parliament enacted a statute that removed various prohibited grounds. This was a feat of legislation known as the Marriage Act, which has descended to the present time. However, there were certainly inadequacies in the law as it existed then and as it has continued to exist up to the present time. Some of these laws and prohibited grounds have touched people very deeply.
I know that several of my colleagues who will be making comments in this debate will be referring to some of the genuine hardships people have suffered as a result of this somewhat antiquated law. However, for those of us who concern ourselves with this law, it has become clear that there is a vagueness in the law as it exists in Canada and there are certain inadequacies which, hopefully, this Bill will meet.
As an example of problems with the current law, there are approximately 30 petitions now before the other place, petitions of individuals who have used their right to petition either a member of the Senate or a Member of the House of Commons asking for relief from some of the prohibited grounds. In my discussions with other Members of Parliament, the number of petitions has increased over the years. I think that is the reason we now have before us the present legislation. The Bill as proposed would remove the need for these petitions.


Marriage Prohibited Degrees Act
The Bill that is presently before us is just the latest attempt to consolidate and update the laws with respect to marriage. There have been several attempts made in the past to achieve this end, and many of us hope that it will not be necessary to make more attempts. There are many of us who hope that this will be perhaps the last kick at the can, so to speak.
The law before us contains a number of measures which I think are helpful. Clause 4 of the Bill states that unless a prohibition is outlined in the law, then all other unions between individuals are all right. The prohibitions that remain fall into two categories. Clause 2(2) states:
No person shall marry another person if they are related
(a)	lineally by consanguinity or adoption-
That is the first category. What that does is to place an absolute prohibition on what we refer to as lineal descendants, one's children, grandchildren or great-grandchildren. Obviously it prohibits marriage between one's parents and one's great-grandparents.
There is one other prohibited category. The Bill states:
No person shall marry another person if they are related-
(b)	as brother and sister by consanguinity, whether by the whole blood or by
the half-blood.
There is an absolute prohibition on marriage between siblings who are related by blood or by the half-blood. That only makes sense. These are prohibitions which we have traditionally frowned upon. Of course, there are genetic reasons as well why society frowns on marriages within those categories.
Hon. Members may have noticed that in the second prohibition there is not a reference to adopted siblings. I suggest that if there is a controversial part in the Bill, and I know that it has been referred to as a housekeeping Bill, it resides in that clause. There are a number of arguments on either side of this issue. One could argue that siblings by adoption have had no choice in their relationship, a parent has made the decision as to what the relationship between the two of them is and therefore there should not be a legal prohibition against their eventual marriage. The trend in provincial law, which has jurisdiction in the area of adoption, is to treat the adopted child as much as possible as a natural child. Most people would agree that that is something that we should pursue. In any case, the committee of the other House that looked at this clause came to the conclusion that at the present time there is not a prohibition against adopted siblings marrying each other.
This matter was studied. A couple appeared before a committee of the other place with a petition asking for permission to marry. Members of the committee looked into the law and concluded that adoption is only a 20th century concept. The law with which we are working was developed in the 19th century and in the centuries before when there was no concept of adoption. Therefore there was no need for this couple to petition the other place because the proposed
marriage was not prohibited. In any event, this is the one area that 1 would like to see looked at again.
Some have pointed to the fact that in Australia the question has been considered. The Australian Government chose to look at the adoptive relationship in exactly the same way as a consanguinity relationship for the purpose of determining capacity to marry. In Australia it was asked why these children should be treated any differently. I believe there is some merit to that argument.
The Bill contains no prohibitions other than the ones I have mentioned. I would suggest that no other prohibitions are necessary. They are not necessary from what we know of genetics. People have gone into the degrees of relationships and have concluded that there is no necessity to prohibit marriage in other categories.
I suggest that social attitudes have changed with respect to how we perceive relationships. As the law stands now, after a divorce one cannot marry one's divorced spouse's uncle or aunt. That is clearly not necessary. Social attitudes have changed in Canada. I think that the number of petitions that are presently before the other place is indicative of that.
We are dealing here with an area that was long within the purview of the churches, and certainly the churches continue to have their laws and rules within their own denominations as to whom they will allow to marry. I think that is all well and good and as it should be. At the same time, I think that we should not attempt to have our civil law conform to the rules of one or more religious denominations. I think most people will agree with that.
To conclude, I believe that the provisions in the Bill are positive. I believe that they are worthy of the attention of the House.

Madam Speaker, I have been motivated to enter this debate on Bill S-5 because of a serious problem that was presented to me by a constituent, a problem that I was incapable of solving because the law needs to be changed in order to solve it. It is her personal problem caused by the present Marriage Act which is prompting me now to speak in this debate and to urge all Hon. Members to consider seriously passing this Bill as quickly as possible.
The Hon. Member for Niagara Falls (Mr. Nicholson) has given an indication to the House that there may be a difficulty with one part of the Bill, the part dealing with adopted children. If that is the case, then I suggest that we deal with that one probable difficulty expeditiously and then bring the Bill back to the House as quickly as possible in order to pass it.
Before I outline the problem of my constituent, I want to commend the Hon. Member for Niagara Falls for being the sponsor of this legislation. He sponsors the Bill from the Senate as a Private Member's Bill. I believe that he is leading the way in helping a considerable number of people in the


country who are facing a problem because of the current Marriage Act. We all recognize that it is necessary and proper that the Marriage Act should prohibit those who are closely related by blood from marrying. That is not what we are talking about here at all. I want to ask the House what sense there is in refusing the right to marry to those who have become related through marriage and that marriage is then dissolved by divorce.
For example, as the Hon. Member for Niagara Falls indicated, the Marriage Act prohibits a woman from marrying her former husband's uncle. I would ask Hon. Members why. What sense is there in that?
Bill S-5 would clarify the law among other situations whereby a person whose marriage has been dissolved by divorce may marry the brother, the sister, the nephew, the niece, the uncle, or the aunt of the divorced spouse.
As has already been indicated, the only procedure available in the past to such couples who wished to be married was to petition Parliament for an exemption. This has been done successfully in the past in quite a number of cases, but the Senate no longer wishes to make such a remedy available. Of course, why should Parliament be burdened with such a cumbersome procedure? How much more logical it is to change the law to make it reasonable and sensible. I am advised, having looked at the time spent in the consideration of Bill S-5, that the Senate has given the Bill the closest possible scrutiny over a considerable period of time. Its purpose, I repeat, is to end confusion in the Marriage Act. It attempts to change the law. These attempts have been under way since 1983, a very long period of time to make what is a straightforward and reasonable change.
The Senate has polled religious groups, legal experts, geneticists, and others, and it has found no serious or major objections to the Bill.
I want to say again that after discussion with the Hon. Member for Niagara Falls and with the Hon. Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson), I recognize the problem already referred to in respect of the provision that a relationship by adoption is no prohibition to marriage, that is, marriage among siblings. I concur fully that we must examine that carefully, but I do not believe that we need to take years to do it. I think that we can do it in a matter of a few weeks at most.
In conclusion, I want to share with the House part of a letter which I received from a constituent so that the House will understand how our refusal to change antiquated laws can create great difficulties and burdens for our citizens. The letter is addressed to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and reads in part:
Dear Sir:
When the House of Commons meets in September, and the Marriage Laws
of Canada are brought up for discussion, your knowledge of my situation
would be greatly appreciated.
Marriage Prohibited Degrees Act
I was married in 1980, and divorced in April of 1986.
I am now engaged to my-(ex-husband's uncle), and I was to be married on August 29th, 1987-
I personally picked up the marriage licence in June. Number 17 on the back of the licence states, "A man may not marry his nephew's wife".
Approximately one week after I picked up the marriage licence, I returned to the town office-and spoke with the Town Clerk-about the validity of number 17. At that time he was unaware of our situation and said he would contact-the Deputy Registrar General in Toronto-
I was told to return our marriage licence for a refund-and then 1 was to be commended on my honesty-
I was informed that the marriage law had been passed through the Senate three times, and all that was required, was a short discussion and a stamp of approval-
Our plans were void. The invitations and the hall had to be cancelled immediately. The marriage licence had to be returned by a friend as a refund of thirty-five dollars seemed to be trivial and embarrassing.
The only hope seemed to be having our banns read in the Church. Some of the laws in the Church are different from the laws of the government.
-(Our priest) told me that if this was the law of the land there was absolutely nothing that he could do.
When the new Constitution of Human Rights came into effect, our Minister, the Bishop, (and ourselves) assumed that an archaic law such as this would be obsolete-
Marriage takes priority in our lives before a family. I am 26, and my (husband-to-be) is 27, we feel that we should be able to make our own decision-.
When the tears stopped, the only alternative was to be married out of our country Canada.
With the help of my Minister and an American Minister, arrangements were made to be married in the U.S.A. Canada considers this to be legal. The laws in the U.S.A. do not pertain to our case-
The House of Commons meets in September. We have decided to explain our situation and hope that in September you will consider us when the House meets again.
It is not our choice to marry in the U.S.A., but if the law is not changed, you leave us no alternative.
We were informed that this law has been brought up for debate since 1983, and we do not want to wait for four more years in case it will never be changed. We were also informed that this law was probably dating back to the 14th Century.
-(We) are literally begging you to take time and change the law in September-
Please take into consideration our situation:. We are not blood related, 1 have been legally divorced for over a year, and my ex-husband has remarried.
The letter ends by indicating that they are looking forward to a favourable reply. It is on the basis of that problem that I rose to speak this afternoon. I hope the House will respond with care and with consideration to the serious problem facing some of our citizens.

Madam Speaker, I am pleased to rise in this debate concerning marriage prohibitions between persons who are too closely related either by consanguinity, affinity or adoption but would like to get married in spite of these prohibitions.
That is a matter that may concern a very small fraction of the population, however it is of very great concern for the people involved. It is easy to understand that marriage


Marriage Prohibited Degrees Act
prohibitions can have great implications in the life of these people on the psychological level.
Since this Bill touches on the perception that we have of the family life, it is vitally important, Madam Speaker, that this House review the matter very carefully.
We must ask ourselves whether our society must continue to be governed by a legislation that is considered by some to be archaic and outdated, given the changes that have happened in our modern Canadian society that is more and more cosmopolitan. For instance, why should a woman be forbidden to marry her uncle or, if she is divorced, her ex-husband's brother or uncle?
To this day couples who were prohibited from marrying each other, especially the first group referred to above, could have their marriage validated if they wished by having the Senate pass a special Bill or an act granting an exception to the general rule. However, in order to do so, these people had to go through a long and difficult process which was also very costly.
For these reasons, the Senate has deemed appropriate to pass Bill S-5, an act to amend and consolidate the laws prohibiting marriage between related persons.
Thus the marriage legislation has been streamlined and made more accessible while still maintaining a number of basic prohibitions.
The only prohibitions that have been kept regarding persons related by consanguinity concern parents, grandparents and children as well as grandchildren and brothers and sisters or half-brother and half-sister. On the other hand, an aunt will be able to marry her nephew and a niece will be able to marry her uncle.
There will no longer be any prohibition concerning persons related by affinity or marriage. The Act also provides that a person whose marriage has been dissolved by divorce can get remarried to the divorced spouse's brother or sister, nephew or niece, uncle or aunt.
In the case of adoption, Bill S-5 prohibits marriage between grandparents, parents, children and grandchildren. That prohibition however would not apply to brothers and sisters by adoption, who would be free to intermarry.
It will always be difficult to have unanimity on those matters, Madam Speaker. Some people would prefer the status quo for reasons of moral, social or religious rectitude. On the other hand, others feel that this area of our legislation should be taken out of the dust of former times and brought into line with this new era, in order to address various situations. Anyway, more often than not, couples will elect to live together in common law marriage if they cannot obtain dispensation from the Senate.
It must be realized, Madam Speaker, that the practice of prohibiting marriage between persons who are related to a certain degree either by consanguinity or adoption stems from
the ancient Judeic religious law, which was enshrined later in a number of statutes adopted under Henry VIII.
So is was that the Canadian provinces which entered Confederation in 1867 adopted that British Common Law tradition. Such is the situation now prevailing in nine provinces out of ten. As far as Quebec is concerned, marriage prohibitions are to be found in Sections 124 to 126 of the Code civil- but they are identical to those in other provinces and those that prevailed at Confederation.
Marriage and divorce are a federal matter under Section 91(26) of the Constitution Act, 1867. And to this day, the law has remained practically unchanged, since the federal Government has elected not to get involved in that area, excepting the Marriage Act, 1970, which only brought in minor amendments.
I will conclude, Madam Speaker, by urging Hon. Members to give particular attention to that matter, in view of its importance to those couples who are looking forward to a legal solution to their problems or who expect an answer that would allow them to clarify their situation.

Mr. Speaker, 1 will be very brief. Bill S-5 was brought before the House by the Hon. Member for Niagara Falls (Mr. Nicholson) and, in my view, is certainly worthy of passage. We in the New Democratic Party are prepared to support the legislation and to see it adopted this afternoon.
It has been subject to a very serious and comprehensive study by the Senate which, as long as it exists, occasionally does some positive, constructive committee work. This is an example of an area in which we are able to benefit from the work done by the Senate. The Senators have heard an extensive number of witnesses and consulted with all the provinces and the two territorial Governments, and we are now able in this Chamber to take advantage of that work.
Having done that, Madam Speaker, I suggest that the time to move forward on this legislation is now, not to delay further the adoption of the legislation.
While I recognize the concern raised by the Hon. Member from Niagara Falls who sponsored the Bill-and I want to pay tribute to him for bringing the Bill before the House-as well as the concern raised by the Hon. Member for Cochrane- Superior (Mr. Penner) with respect to adopted siblings, I do want to make it very clear that while we recognize those concerns, we are prepared to see the legislation adopted in all stages this afternoon.

speechtext: The Hon. Member for La Prairie (Mr. Jourdenais) on a point of order.

Madam Speaker, 1 simply want to point out to my colleagues in the House and to all Canadians-

-that I was present in the Chamber when the vote on Bill C-84 took place.

-and that I abstained from the vote for reasons which many people already know. There is no need to explain them.

Also, my conscience did not permit me to act otherwise.
Hear, hear!

dissolve Canagrex and to amend certain Acts in consequence thereof, be read the third time and passed.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Madam Speaker, 1 wonder if you would seek the sense of the House as to whether it would care to have the vote as recorded on the Bill we have just dealt with apply to this one on the understanding that each vote would be recorded separately.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Is the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis) seeking the floor?
No, Madam Speaker, I am not seeking the floor.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: 1 imagine that the House can well understand that the Chair did not know whether or not the Hon. Member was seeking the floor. He was neither sitting nor standing.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That's their position.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Am I to understand that there is unanimous consent to apply the vote?
Agreed.
